title: TaskCompletionSource
sub: Your own task from callbacks: completion, unsubscribing, cancellation and continuations
cards/0/body:
TaskCompletionSource<T> creates a Task<T> with no body. Nobody runs it, and no thread waits on it. You complete the task yourself, from the outside, in one of three ways, one per final state (section 1):

  • SetResult(x): success with a result;
  • SetException(e): an error (Faulted), await will throw e;
  • SetCanceled(): cancellation (Canceled), await will throw OperationCanceledException.

This is how an old callback- or event-based API becomes a task you can await. Step by step:

  • 1. GetLocationAsync subscribes to the events, starts the GPS and immediately returns the unfinished tcs.Task.
  • 2. The caller awaits: the task isn't ready, so the method registers its continuation and returns. The thread is free while the GPS looks for satellites.
  • 3. The GPS library raises OnFix on its own thread, and the handler calls SetResult.
  • 4. The task is complete, and the caller's continuation starts. Exactly where is the main catch of this lesson; more on it below.
cards/1/options/0: Completes tcs.Task with a result, and everyone awaiting it continues
cards/1/options/2: Blocks the thread until someone takes the result
cards/1/explain: A TaskCompletionSource task doesn't run anything itself: it's completed from the outside. SetResult moves it to a final state and starts the continuations of whoever is waiting.
cards/2/q: Which line can leave the task hanging forever?
cards/2/explain: On an error the handler only logs it, and nobody completes the task: the await will wait forever. You need tcs.SetException(e).
cards/3/body:
A task completes once. A second SetResult, SetException or SetCanceled throws InvalidOperationException ("An attempt was made to transition a task to a final state when it had already completed"). Each has a Try version: TrySetResult, TrySetException, TrySetCanceled. If the task is already complete, the Try version does nothing and returns false.

There are usually several sources of completion: a success event, an error event, cancellation. They can fire almost at once or more than once: a GPS may well send OnFix twice. The first one wins, and the other Try calls quietly return false. That's why code like this uses only the Try versions.

The code below has three sources: OnFix, OnError and cancellation by token. How the unsubscribing and the cancellation work is in the card after the question.
cards/4/q: Why does GetLocationAsync(ct) use TrySetResult rather than SetResult?
cards/4/options/0: The event may arrive twice or after cancellation: SetResult on a completed task throws InvalidOperationException, while TrySetResult returns false
cards/4/options/1: TrySetResult waits until the task is ready to accept a result, while SetResult throws right away
cards/4/options/2: SetResult can be called only from the thread that created the task
cards/4/explain: A task completes once. With several sources of completion, the first one wins, and the other Try calls quietly return false. A second SetResult would throw right on the library's thread, inside its event handler.
cards/5/title: Clean up after yourself: unsubscribing and cancellation
cards/5/body:
Besides the Try versions, GetLocationAsync(ct) has two more duties:

  • Unsubscribe from the events. Otherwise the source holds the handlers, and through them tcs, forever. Every call adds more of them, and all of them fire on every event. The unsubscribing sits in a finally: it runs whatever the await ends with.
  • Hook up cancellation. ct.Register(callback) subscribes a callback to the token's cancellation: Cancel() calls the subscribers (section 2). If the token is already canceled, Register calls the callback right away. The callback completes the task with TrySetCanceled(ct). Register returns a registration, and using removes the subscription when the method ends. A timeout is the same token, just from a CancellationTokenSource with a timeout.

Every path step by step is in the code below.
cards/6/q: In GetLocationAsync(ct) the token is canceled before OnFix arrives. What does the caller get?
cards/6/options/0: await throws OperationCanceledException: Cancel called the Register callback, and it called TrySetCanceled
cards/6/options/1: The task keeps waiting for OnFix: a token only affects methods that accept it
cards/6/explain: Register subscribed a callback to cancellation. Cancel calls the subscribers, the callback moves the task to Canceled, and await throws OperationCanceledException (more precisely, its subclass TaskCanceledException). finally unsubscribes the events, and using removes the registration.
cards/6/wrong/1: Without Register that's what would happen: the TaskCompletionSource task knows nothing about the token. Register is exactly what connects it to cancellation.
cards/6/wrong/2: A canceled task has no value to return: await throws.
cards/7/q: The finally with the unsubscribing was removed from GetLocationAsync(ct), and the method is called on every screen. What happens after a hundred calls?
cards/7/options/0: gps accumulates a hundred pairs of handlers: each holds its own tcs, and all of them fire on every event
cards/7/explain: A subscription is a reference from gps to the handler, and through it to tcs and everything it captured. Without unsubscribing, the GC can't collect them. The old handlers call TrySetResult on long-completed tasks and get false: no errors you can see, just a leak and extra work on every event.
cards/7/wrong/1: The old handlers call the Try versions, and on a completed task those return false instead of throwing. SetResult would throw, right inside the library's event handler.
cards/7/wrong/2: A new call subscribes its own handlers, and the very first event completes its task.
cards/8/title: The catch: continuations run inside SetResult
cards/8/body:
Remember section 4: with no context, a continuation usually runs synchronously on the thread that completed the task. A TaskCompletionSource task is completed by your SetResult. So the waiting method's continuation (its MoveNext) runs right inside SetResult, on the thread that called it. SetResult returns only when that method reaches its next real pause or its end.

  • The waiter captured a UI context, and SetResult was called from another thread: the continuation goes via Post to the UI thread's queue, and SetResult returns right away.
  • The waiter has no context (console, ASP.NET Core, a pool thread, ConfigureAwait(false)): the continuation runs right there, inside SetResult.

Why this is dangerous: someone else's code runs on the library's thread and under its locks. While it runs, the library is stuck. If it calls into the library again, it re-enters the library's lock (Monitor is reentrant, previous lesson) while the library's state is half-done. If it synchronously waits for something that needs that lock on another thread, you get a deadlock.

The flag from the GetLocationAsync(ct) code turns this off; more on it after the question.
cards/9/q: ASP.NET Core, a TaskCompletionSource created without the flag. The library calls SetResult on its own thread under its own lock. Where and when does the request's code after await tcs.Task run?
cards/9/options/0: Right away, inside SetResult: on the library's thread and under its lock
cards/9/options/1: On a pool thread, after SetResult returns
cards/9/options/2: On the request's thread, which has been waiting for the task all along
cards/9/explain: ASP.NET Core has no context, and there's no flag either. The continuation runs synchronously on the thread that completed the task: the library's thread, inside its lock.
cards/9/wrong/1: That's what would happen with the RunContinuationsAsynchronously flag.
cards/9/wrong/2: No thread was waiting for the task: the method returned at the await, and the thread went off to serve other requests.
cards/10/body:
The TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously flag in the constructor changes step 3 from the previous card: continuations don't run inside SetResult but are queued (to the pool or via Post to the captured context), and SetResult returns right away. The waiter's code runs on another thread, outside the library's locks. Use it by default for TaskCompletionSource: the price is one extra hop through a queue.

A naming trap: the TaskContinuationOptions enum has a member with the same name. new TaskCompletionSource<T>(TaskContinuationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously) compiles because the value goes to the overload with an object state parameter, and it turns nothing on. The CA2247 analyzer warns about this.
cards/11/q: The flag is there, but continuations still run inside TrySetResult. Which line is to blame?
cards/11/explain: TaskCompletionSource has no overload that takes TaskContinuationOptions: the value silently goes to the object state parameter. You need TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously. This is exactly what the CA2247 analyzer catches.
cards/12/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/12/options/1: TrySetResult on a completed task returns false
cards/12/options/2: A TaskCompletionSource task has no body: it's completed from the outside
cards/12/options/3: Dispose on a TaskCompletionSource cancels the task
cards/12/options/4: RunContinuationsAsynchronously runs the task on a separate thread
cards/12/explain: TaskCompletionSource has no Dispose at all: you cancel through SetCanceled or TrySetCanceled. And the flag only affects where the waiters' continuations run: there's nobody to run the task itself.
cards/13/pairs/0/1: A task with no body that you complete yourself
cards/13/pairs/1/1: Complete it if it isn't complete yet
cards/13/pairs/2/1: Call a callback when the token is canceled
